# Data efficiency on HiLiftAeroML {#sec-data-efficiency}

Trained on 35 high-lift wing cases, ISLA predicts surface
pressure 2.8x more accurately than GeoTransolver and than plain Transolver;
at 210 cases the advantage is 2.2x over GeoTransolver and 1.3x over
Transolver; at 1,260 cases ISLA and GeoTransolver are at parity (Transolver
was not run at that rung). The result
is specific to HiLiftAeroML: on DrivAerML, where the freestream is fixed,
GeoTransolver is 1.2–1.3x more accurate than ISLA from 27 training cases up
(@sec-de-drivaerml). This chapter states exactly what was measured, shows
that the HiLift result holds case by case and under every steel-man control
constructed for the baselines, translates it into force-coefficient
accuracy, and reports what the program has learned about *what* carries it —
which is less than one would like. Every ratio between architectures in this
chapter is the baseline's error divided by ISLA's, so a value above one favours
ISLA. The chapter's limits are stated in @sec-de-limits and collected with the
rest of the book's in @sec-limits.

## What was measured {#sec-de-setup}

HiLiftAeroML (@sec-datasets) holds 1,800 cases: 180 high-lift wing
geometries, each simulated at ten angles of attack from 4° to 22°. Its
curated data-efficiency splits are nested — 35 training cases inside 210
inside 510 inside 1,260 — and all four share one 180-case validation set
and one sealed 360-case test set (@sec-splits). The training subsets are
random draws from the 1,260-case pool, so the 35-case split contains 3–7
cases at each angle except 18°, of which it has none, and 33 distinct
geometries.

The quantity reported is the relative L2 error of surface pressure on the
validation cases (@sec-metrics): for one case, the norm of the error over
its 10,000 sampled surface points divided by the norm of the true field on
the same points, then the arithmetic mean over the 180 cases. Every
architecture is trained under the same frozen protocol (@sec-protocol):
10,000 sampled surface points per case, 500 epochs, bfloat16, no
augmentation, two seeds, and the learning rate each architecture prefers
on the full split (1e-3 for ISLA and GeoTransolver; Transolver, which had
no prior tuning on this dataset, was run at 1e-3 and 3e-3 and is reported
at the better of the two per rung, 3e-3). The final-epoch checkpoint of each
run is evaluated; no checkpoint is selected on validation error, and the
validation set was otherwise used only for the learning-rate choice on the
full split. Resources are matched in parameters (8.9M for ISLA against 9.0M
for GeoTransolver and 6.0M for Transolver) and tokens per case; peak
training memory at this token count is 1.5 GB for ISLA against 4.6 GB for
GeoTransolver (@sec-resource-matching). The test split was never read;
every number in this chapter is a validation-set number.

## The result {#sec-de-result}

```{python}
#| label: fig-hilift-data-efficiency
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Surface-pressure relative L2 error on the shared 180-case validation set
#|   versus number of training cases, for GeoTransolver (red circles),
#|   ISLA (blue squares) and plain Transolver without a geometry
#|   encoder (grey triangles, dashed; at its better learning rate, 3e-3).
#|   Lines join seed means, shaded bands span the seeds (three at 35 and 210
#|   cases, two at 1,260), small dots are the individual seeds. The annotated factors are each baseline's error
#|   divided by ISLA's at the same rung (above one favours ISLA). Protocol: 10,000 sampled surface
#|   points per case, 500 epochs, bfloat16, no augmentation, learning rate
#|   1e-3 for GeoTransolver and ISLA; ISLA in its constant-gauge
#|   configuration. The figure does not show scaling beyond 1,260 cases and does not show
#|   DrivAerML, where the ordering reverses (@tbl-drivaerml-dataeff-ladder). Data:
#|   results/hilift_ladder_reduction_2026-09-03.json,
#|   results/t1_transolver_control_reduction_2026-09-05.json,
#|   results/w2_reduction_2026-09-07b.json (third seeds).
#| code-fold: true
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib as mpl
BLUE, RED, GREY = "#2a78d6", "#e34948", "#52514e"
INK, INK2, MUTED, GRID, BASELINE = "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#898781", "#e1e0d9", "#c3c2b7"
mpl.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "font.size": 10, "axes.edgecolor": BASELINE,
                     "axes.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.grid": True, "grid.color": GRID,
                     "xtick.color": MUTED, "ytick.color": MUTED, "xtick.labelcolor": INK2,
                     "ytick.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.spines.top": False,
                     "axes.spines.right": False, "legend.frameon": False})
lad = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "hilift_ladder_reduction_2026-09-03.json"))
t1 = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "t1_transolver_control_reduction_2026-09-05.json"))
w2 = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "w2_reduction_2026-09-07b.json"))["runs"]
lad = {**lad, **{k: v for k, v in w2.items() if k.startswith("lad_hl_")}}
t1 = {**t1, **{k: v for k, v in w2.items() if k.startswith("t1_hl_transolver")}}
rungs = [(35, "lad_hl_{a}_super_scarce_seed{s}"), (210, "lad_hl_{a}_scarce_seed{s}"), (1260, "{a}_hl_lr1_seed{s}")]
data = {}
for arch in ("gt", "mt2"):
    xs, means, lo, hi, pts = [], [], [], [], []
    for n, pat in rungs:
        v = [lad[pat.format(a=arch, s=s)]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43, 44) if pat.format(a=arch, s=s) in lad]
        xs.append(n); means.append(statistics.mean(v)); lo.append(min(v)); hi.append(max(v)); pts.append(v)
    data[arch] = (xs, means, lo, hi, pts)
xs, means, lo, hi, pts = [], [], [], [], []
for n, pat in [(35, "t1_hl_transolver_super_scarce_{lr}_seed{s}"), (210, "t1_hl_transolver_scarce_{lr}_seed{s}")]:
    best = None
    for lr in ("lr1e3", "lr3e3"):
        v = [t1[pat.format(lr=lr, s=s)]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43, 44) if pat.format(lr=lr, s=s) in t1]
        if len(v) >= 2 and (best is None or statistics.mean(v) < statistics.mean(best)):
            best = v
    xs.append(n); means.append(statistics.mean(best)); lo.append(min(best)); hi.append(max(best)); pts.append(best)
data["t"] = (xs, means, lo, hi, pts)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 5.0))
style = {"gt": (RED, "o", "-", 2.2), "t": (GREY, "^", "--", 1.6), "mt2": (BLUE, "s", "-", 2.2)}
for arch in ("gt", "t", "mt2"):
    xs, means, lo, hi, pts = data[arch]; c, mk, ls, lw = style[arch]
    ax.fill_between(xs, lo, hi, color=c, alpha=0.18, lw=0)
    ax.plot(xs, means, color=c, lw=lw, ls=ls, marker=mk, ms=7, zorder=3)
    for x, v in zip(xs, pts):
        ax.scatter([x] * len(v), v, color=c, s=14, alpha=0.9, zorder=4)
ax.annotate("GeoTransolver", (35, data["gt"][1][0]), xytext=(14, 2), textcoords="offset points", color=RED, fontweight="bold", va="center",
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.85))
ax.annotate("ISLA", (210, data["mt2"][1][1]), xytext=(14, -14), textcoords="offset points", color=BLUE, fontweight="bold", va="center",
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.85))
xm, ym = (35 * 210) ** 0.5, (data["t"][1][0] * data["t"][1][1]) ** 0.5
ax.annotate("Transolver", (xm, ym), xytext=(-3, -7), textcoords="offset points", color=GREY, fontsize=9.5, ha="right", va="top",
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.85))
for i, n in enumerate((35, 210)):
    r_gt = data["gt"][1][i] / data["mt2"][1][i]; r_t = data["t"][1][i] / data["mt2"][1][i]
    ymid = (data["gt"][1][i] * data["mt2"][1][i]) ** 0.5
    ax.annotate("", (n, data["mt2"][1][i]), (n, data["gt"][1][i]), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=INK2, lw=0.9, shrinkA=4, shrinkB=4))
    ax.text(n * 1.08, ymid, f"GeoTransolver {r_gt:.1f}x ISLA\nTransolver {r_t:.1f}x ISLA", color=INK2, fontsize=9, va="center", linespacing=1.3,
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.85))
r_full = data["gt"][1][2] / data["mt2"][1][2]
ax.annotate(f"{r_full:.2f}x (parity)", (1260, (data["gt"][1][2] * data["mt2"][1][2]) ** 0.5), xytext=(14, 30), textcoords="offset points", color=INK2, fontsize=9, va="bottom")
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xticks([35, 210, 1260]); ax.set_xticklabels(["35", "210", "1,260"])
ax.set_yticks([0.04, 0.06, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4]); ax.set_yticklabels(["0.04", "0.06", "0.10", "0.20", "0.40"])
ax.set_xlim(22, 3200)
ax.set_xlabel("Training cases [count]", color=INK2)
ax.set_ylabel("Surface pressure error, rel-L2 [–]", color=INK2)
ax.set_title("Data efficiency on HiLiftAeroML (shared 180-case validation set)", color=INK, loc="left", fontsize=11, pad=10)
ax.grid(True, which="major", color=GRID); ax.grid(False, which="minor")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-hilift-ladder
#| output: asis
#| code-fold: true
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
lad = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "hilift_ladder_reduction_2026-09-03.json"))
t1 = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "t1_transolver_control_reduction_2026-09-05.json"))
w2 = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "w2_reduction_2026-09-07b.json"))["runs"]
lad = {**lad, **{k: v for k, v in w2.items() if k.startswith("lad_hl_")}}
t1 = {**t1, **{k: v for k, v in w2.items() if k.startswith("t1_hl_transolver")}}
inv = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "inv_transplant_2026-09-07.json"))
def pair(d, pat):
    v = [d[pat.format(s=s)]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43, 44) if pat.format(s=s) in d]
    return v
rows = []
for n, gpat, mpat, tpat in [(35, "lad_hl_gt_super_scarce_seed{s}", "lad_hl_mt2_super_scarce_seed{s}", "t1_hl_transolver_super_scarce_lr3e3_seed{s}"),
                            (210, "lad_hl_gt_scarce_seed{s}", "lad_hl_mt2_scarce_seed{s}", "t1_hl_transolver_scarce_lr3e3_seed{s}"),
                            (1260, "gt_hl_lr1_seed{s}", "mt2_hl_lr1_seed{s}", None)]:
    g, m = pair(lad, gpat), pair(lad, mpat)
    t = pair(t1, tpat) if tpat else []
    gm, mm = statistics.mean(g), statistics.mean(m)
    tcell = f"{statistics.mean(t):.3f} ({min(t):.3f}–{max(t):.3f})" if t else "—"
    tr = f"{statistics.mean(t)/mm:.1f}" if t else "—"
    rows.append(f"| {n:,} | {gm:.3f} ({min(g):.3f}–{max(g):.3f}) | {tcell} | **{mm:.3f}** ({min(m):.3f}–{max(m):.3f}) | {gm/mm:.2f} | {tr} |")
print("| training cases | GeoTransolver | Transolver (lr 3e-3) | ISLA | GT / ISLA | T / ISLA |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---|---|")
print("\n".join(rows))
print()
print(": Surface-pressure relative L2 error on the shared 180-case validation set: seed mean (seed range) for each architecture at each rung, and the ratio of each baseline's mean to ISLA's. Ratios above 1 mean ISLA is more accurate. Same protocol and sources as @fig-hilift-data-efficiency. {#tbl-hilift-ladder}")
```

Two features of the numbers matter before any interpretation. The seed
spreads are small against the gaps at 35 and 210 cases (0.006 for ISLA and
0.035 for GeoTransolver against a gap of 0.25 at 35 cases), and the gap
closes monotonically with data: 2.8x, then 2.2x, then parity. GeoTransolver
reaches the accuracy ISLA has at 210 cases somewhere between 210 and 1,260
cases (the 510-case rung is not yet measured).

The same-family control sharpens the statement rather than weakening it.
Plain Transolver — GeoTransolver's attention family without the geometry
encoder — collapses exactly like GeoTransolver at 35 cases (0.40, 2.9x ISLA)
but recovers faster, reaching 0.086 at 210 cases, where it is 1.8x more
accurate than GeoTransolver itself. So at 210 cases most of the 2.2x gap
to GeoTransolver is GeoTransolver's geometry encoder falling behind its own
backbone, and ISLA's advantage over the *best* Transolver-family baseline is
1.3x. At 35 cases the two baselines are indistinguishable and the 2.8x
holds against both.

## It holds case by case {#sec-de-paired}

The 180 validation cases are shared, so each can be scored once as a
paired comparison: for every case, each architecture's two-seed mean error
(@sec-metrics). The table reports how many of the 180 cases ISLA wins, how
many it wins on both seeds individually (a stricter count), an exact
two-sided sign test on n = 180, and the distribution of the per-case error
ratio.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-hilift-paired
#| output: asis
#| code-fold: true
import json
from pathlib import Path
ps = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "hilift_paired_stats_case_2026-09-07.json"))
names = {"gt": "GeoTransolver", "transolver": "Transolver (lr 3e-3)"}
print("| training cases | baseline | cases ISLA wins (of 180) | wins on both seeds | sign-test p (n = 180) | median ratio (baseline / ISLA) | 10th–90th percentile |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|")
for n in ("35", "210", "1260"):
    for b in ("gt", "transolver"):
        k = f"mt2_vs_{b}"
        if k not in ps[n]:
            continue
        r = ps[n][k]
        print(f"| {int(n):,} | {names[b]} | **{r['mt2_wins_seed_mean']} / {r['n_cases']}** | {r['mt2_wins_both_seeds']} | {r['sign_test_p_n180']:.0e} | {r['median_ratio_base_over_mt2']:.2f} | {r['q10_ratio']:.2f}–{r['q90_ratio']:.2f} |")
print()
print(": Case-level paired comparison on the 180 shared validation cases. Each case is scored once by each architecture's two-seed mean pressure error; 'wins' counts cases where ISLA's error is lower, and the next column counts cases where ISLA is lower on each seed separately. The sign test is exact and two-sided against a 50% null on n = 180. Ratios are baseline error over ISLA error; above 1 favours ISLA. Data: results/hilift_paired_stats_case_2026-09-07.json. {#tbl-hilift-paired}")
```

At 35 cases there is no validation case, on either seed, where either
baseline beats ISLA, and the worst tenth of cases still favour ISLA by 1.8x.
At 210 cases ISLA wins 177 of 180 cases against GeoTransolver (175 on both
seeds) and 165 of 180 against Transolver (median 1.5x). At 1,260 cases,
where the means are at parity, ISLA is lower on 130 of 180 cases (103 on
both seeds) with a median ratio of 1.06 — a small per-case edge the mean
comparison hides, and one that the paired view is the right instrument to
see.

The same per-case errors answer a second question: do the two architectures
agree on *which* cases are hard? @tbl-hilift-percase-rho gives the Spearman
rank correlation between ISLA's and GeoTransolver's per-case errors at each
rung, next to each architecture's rank correlation with its own second seed,
which is the ceiling a correlation between two models could reach.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-hilift-percase-rho
#| output: asis
#| code-fold: true
import json
from pathlib import Path
hl = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "hilift_percase_correlation_2026-09-07.json"))
dr = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "drivaer_percase_correlation_2026-09-07.json"))
print("| dataset and rung | cases | ρ ISLA vs GeoTransolver | ρ GeoTransolver, seed vs seed | ρ ISLA, seed vs seed | per-case ratio GeoTransolver / ISLA, 10th / 50th / 90th pct |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---|---|")
for key, label in (("35", "HiLiftAeroML, 35"), ("210", "HiLiftAeroML, 210"), ("1260", "HiLiftAeroML, 1,260"), ("single12", "HiLiftAeroML, single angle, 126 (18 held-out geometries)")):
    r = hl[key]; p = r["ratio_gt_over_isla_p10_p50_p90"]
    print(f"| {label} | {r['n']} | **{r['rho_isla_vs_gt']:.2f}** | {r['rho_gt_self']:.2f} | {r['rho_isla_self']:.2f} | {p[0]:.2f} / {p[1]:.2f} / {p[2]:.2f} |")
for s in ("45", "46"):
    r = dr[s]; p = [1 / x for x in reversed(r["ratio_p10_p50_p90"])]
    print(f"| DrivAerML, 435 (seed pair {s}) | {r['n']} | **{r['spearman_isla_vs_gt_per_case_pressure_l2']:.2f}** | {dr['self_consistency']['gt_seed45_vs_46']:.2f} | {dr['self_consistency']['isla_seed45_vs_46']:.2f} | {p[0]:.2f} / {p[1]:.2f} / {p[2]:.2f} |")
print()
print(": Do the architectures agree on which cases are hard? Spearman rank correlation of per-case surface-pressure error between ISLA and GeoTransolver (two-seed means per case on HiLiftAeroML; single seeds on DrivAerML, where the same-numbered seeds are paired), against each architecture's correlation with its own other seed. Ratios are GeoTransolver error over ISLA error per case (above 1 favours ISLA); on DrivAerML the artifact stores ISLA/GeoTransolver and the table inverts it. Data: results/hilift_percase_correlation_2026-09-07.json, results/drivaer_percase_correlation_2026-09-07.json. {#tbl-hilift-percase-rho}")
```

Each architecture is consistent with itself (0.87–0.97 across seeds), so the
cross-architecture correlations are resolved. At 35 and 210 cases they are
0.57 and 0.64, and the per-case ratio spans 1.8x to 4.6x; at 1,260 cases
the two orderings coincide (0.94, the seed ceiling) and the ratio collapses
to 0.92–1.18. On DrivAerML the orderings coincide at every size (0.86–0.89)
and GeoTransolver's edge is a near-constant factor. The reason the
orderings differ at small data is not that GeoTransolver fails on cases of
its own: its error barely varies by case at all. At 35 cases the
coefficient of variation of GeoTransolver's per-case error is 0.15 against
ISLA's 0.44, and at 210 cases 0.19 against 0.64; both models' errors rise
with angle of attack (rank correlation 0.56 and 0.61 at 35 cases), and
neither tracks how far a case's field is from uniform
(results/hilift_error_drivers_2026-09-07.json). GeoTransolver at small data
is a nearly case-independent predictor, which is what @sec-de-strata reads
from the reference predictors; ISLA's error varies three to four times
more across cases because it has learned the case-to-case physics, and a
model that has cannot be rank-correlated with one that has not.

A third seed at 35 cases gives ISLA 0.138, GeoTransolver 0.359 and Transolver
0.409. ISLA's third seed falls inside its two-seed range (0.135–0.141);
GeoTransolver's falls below its range (0.375–0.409) and Transolver's just
above (0.398–0.406). The three-seed means are 0.138, 0.381 and 0.404, for
factors of 2.8x and 2.9x. At 210 cases the third seed gives ISLA 0.0657
and Transolver 0.0875, each inside its two-seed range, and GeoTransolver
0.107, far below its two-seed range of 0.157–0.160: GeoTransolver's three
seeds at 210 cases span a factor of 1.5 (0.107–0.160) where ISLA's and
Transolver's span 1.07. The three-seed means are 0.0648, 0.141 and 0.087,
for factors of 2.2x and 1.3x, and those are the 210-case factors this
book states (results/w2_reduction_2026-09-07b.json). GeoTransolver's
small-data results on this dataset are seed-fragile in a way the other
two architectures' are not, which fits its flat, geometry-blind error at
these sizes (@tbl-hilift-percase-rho): which basin the optimizer lands in
matters more than which cases it sees.

## Where the advantage lives {#sec-de-strata}

Two hypotheses about a small-data advantage make different predictions
about where on the validation set it appears. If it came from memorizing
geometries, it should collapse on validation geometries that the 35
training cases never contain; if it came from interpolating angle of
attack, it should collapse at the one angle (18°) the training set lacks.
The table stratifies the 35-case results by both.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-hilift-strata
#| output: asis
#| code-fold: true
import json
from pathlib import Path
st = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "hilift_stratified_35_2026-09-06.json"))
print("| angle of attack [deg] | training cases at this angle | validation cases | ISLA | GeoTransolver | Transolver | GT / ISLA |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|")
for aoa in sorted(st["by_aoa"], key=int):
    r = st["by_aoa"][aoa]
    bold = "**" if r["n_train"] == 0 else ""
    print(f"| {bold}{aoa}{bold} | {r['n_train']} | {r['n_val']} | {r['mt2']:.3f} | {r['gt']:.3f} | {r['transolver']:.3f} | {r['gt']/r['mt2']:.1f} |")
print()
print(": The 35-case models stratified by angle of attack: geometric-mean pressure rel-L2 over the validation cases at each angle (both seeds). The 18° row (bold) is an angle absent from the 35 training cases. Data: results/hilift_stratified_35_2026-09-06.json. {#tbl-hilift-strata}")
print()
print("| validation geometry seen in training at another angle | validation cases | ISLA | GeoTransolver | Transolver | GT / ISLA |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---|---|")
for k, lab in (("True", "yes"), ("False", "**no**")):
    r = st["by_geometry_seen"][k]
    print(f"| {lab} | {r['n_val']} | {r['mt2']:.3f} | {r['gt']:.3f} | {r['transolver']:.3f} | {r['gt']/r['mt2']:.1f} |")
print()
print(": The same models stratified by whether the validation geometry appears among the 33 geometries of the 35-case training set. Data: results/hilift_stratified_35_2026-09-06.json. {#tbl-hilift-strata-geo}")
```

Neither collapse happens. On the 146 never-seen geometries ISLA is 3.0x
ahead; seeing a geometry at another angle helps ISLA by 15% and
GeoTransolver not at all, and at 210 cases GeoTransolver is again identical
on seen and unseen geometries (0.158 against 0.159) while ISLA no longer
needs to have seen one (0.066 against 0.061;
results/hilift_seen_vs_unseen_geometry_2026-09-07.json). Together with the
per-case decorrelation of @tbl-hilift-percase-rho, this rules out
memorization or local interpolation in geometry space as GeoTransolver's
small-data behaviour: it does not exploit the geometries it has seen. At 18°, ISLA interpolates smoothly between its
16° and 20° errors (0.135 → 0.167 → 0.186) and stays 2.5x ahead. The
advantage is uniform — 2.2x to 4.3x at every angle — and largest in
attached flow (4°–12°), where ISLA's error is 0.09–0.10 against 0.33–0.39
for the baselines.

The strictest version of the geometry question removes the seen geometries
altogether. Trained on 40 cases made of only four geometries at all ten
angles, and validated on the 180 cases of 18 geometries that appear in no
training set at any angle, ISLA reaches 0.248 and 0.251 (two seeds) against
GeoTransolver's 0.407 and 0.492: 1.8x on pressure, 1.9x on velocity, 1.7x on
wall shear, and 172 of 180 cases (158 on both seeds; median per-case ratio
2.24; results/w2_reduction_2026-09-07b.json,
results/hilift_paired_stats_case_2026-09-07b.json). Two things in these
numbers matter beyond the ratio. ISLA's error nearly doubles relative to the
35-case random split (0.138 → 0.250) when the number of distinct training
geometries falls from 33 to 4 at a similar case count, so its accuracy is
paid for in geometries, not cases; GeoTransolver's error barely changes
(0.39 → 0.45) and its two seeds disagree by 20%. The advantage on never-seen
geometries is therefore real and case-by-case, and it is smaller than at the
random split because ISLA, not GeoTransolver, responds to geometry
diversity.

The strata also show *what kind* of model each is at 35 cases. The
baselines' error is nearly flat — 0.33 to 0.47 at every angle, identical on
seen and unseen geometries — while ISLA's tracks the physics, doubling from
attached flow to post-stall. Against reference predictors on the same
cases (a constant freestream pressure everywhere scores 1.00 on the
gauge-pressure scale, the dataset mean 0.94, each case's own mean 0.93),
GeoTransolver scores 0.63 and Transolver 0.68 while ISLA scores 0.25; the
median per-case correlation between predicted and true pressure is 0.76
and 0.69 for the baselines against 0.97 for ISLA
^[`results/hilift_reference_predictors_35_2026-09-06.json`]. At 35 cases the
baselines have learned the coarse, case-independent pressure pattern and
about half of the case-to-case variation; ISLA has learned most of it.

## In engineering terms: lift and drag {#sec-de-forces}

Integrating the predicted pressure and wall shear over each wing gives
its lift and drag coefficients. The table reports the mean absolute error
of each coefficient over the 180 validation cases, relative to the mean
magnitude of the true coefficient (the recipe integrates with a unit
reference area, so only relative errors are meaningful).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-hilift-forces
#| output: asis
#| code-fold: true
import json
from pathlib import Path
ps = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "hilift_paired_stats_2026-09-06.json"))
names = {"mt2": "ISLA", "gt": "GeoTransolver", "transolver": "Transolver (lr 3e-3)"}
print("| training cases | architecture | drag coefficient error | lift coefficient error |")
print("|---|---|---|---|")
for n in ("35", "210", "1260"):
    for a in ("mt2", "gt", "transolver"):
        f = ps[n]["forces"].get(a)
        if not f:
            continue
        b = "**" if a == "mt2" and n == "35" else ""
        print(f"| {int(n):,} | {names[a]} | {b}{100*f['CD']['rel_mae']:.1f}%{b} | {b}{100*f['CL']['rel_mae']:.1f}%{b} |")
print()
print(": Force-coefficient error: mean absolute error of the integrated drag (CD) and lift (CL) coefficients over the 180 validation cases, as a percentage of the mean magnitude of the true coefficient, averaged over seeds. Data: results/hilift_paired_stats_2026-09-06.json. {#tbl-hilift-forces}")
```

From 35 CFD runs, ISLA predicts the lift and drag of unseen high-lift
configurations to about 3%, where GeoTransolver reaches 11–17% and
Transolver 8–12%. At 210 runs all three are within 1.5–3%, and at 1,260
the two-seed means are indistinguishable. The 3% figure is the practical
content of this chapter: a few-dozen-run design-of-experiments budget
yields a force surrogate of usable accuracy.

## Steel-man controls {#sec-de-controls}

A small-data advantage can be a protocol artefact: the fixed 500-epoch
budget gives a 35-case model only 4,500 optimizer steps, and the learning
rate was chosen on the full split. Four GeoTransolver controls test both
explanations, with the preregistered falsifier that any control within
1.2x of ISLA at 35 cases voids the result.

| training cases | GeoTransolver control | error (seed 42 / seed 43) | GeoTransolver at the protocol rate and epochs | falsifier (1.2x ISLA) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 35 | learning rate 3e-3, 500 epochs | 0.392 / 0.480 | 0.375 / 0.409 | 0.166 |
| 35 | learning rate 1e-3, 1,000 epochs | 0.373 / 0.429 | 0.375 / 0.409 | 0.166 |
| 210 | learning rate 3e-3, 500 epochs | 0.220 / 0.290 | 0.157 / 0.160 | 0.077 |
| 210 | learning rate 1e-3, 1,000 epochs | 0.152 / 0.128 | 0.157 / 0.160 | 0.077 |

: GeoTransolver steel-man controls, two seeds each, on the shared validation set. A higher learning rate hurts at both rungs; doubling the epochs helps only at 210 cases (0.140 against 0.159, 1.13x) and leaves GeoTransolver 2.2x behind ISLA there. No control approaches the falsifier. Data: results/t1_transolver_control_reduction_2026-09-05.json. {#tbl-hilift-controls}

The same-family baseline (Transolver at its better learning rate) is a
further control, already in the tables above. A learning-rate explanation is
also implausible on independent grounds:
GeoTransolver's sensitivity to learning rate is itself one of the measured
differences between the architectures (@sec-robustness-lr).

## A free uncertainty signal {#sec-de-uq}

Because two seeds exist for every model, the disagreement between them is
a per-case uncertainty estimate at no extra cost. Its rank correlation
with the per-case error tells whether a model knows where it is wrong.

| training cases | ISLA | GeoTransolver | Transolver |
|---|---|---|---|
| 35 | **+0.67** | −0.20 | −0.47 |
| 210 | +0.64 | +0.65 | +0.60 |
| 1,260 | +0.15 | +0.19 | — |

: Spearman rank correlation, over the 180 validation cases, between the two seeds' disagreement (norm of the difference of their pressure predictions) and the two-seed ensemble's error. Data: results/hilift_ensemble_uq_{35,210,1260}_2026-09-06.json. {#tbl-hilift-uq}

At 35 cases ISLA's seed disagreement ranks its errors (0.67), so a two-seed
ISLA ships with a usable per-case confidence flag; the baselines'
disagreement is anticorrelated with their error, so an ensemble spread
would mislead. At 210 cases all three architectures have the property,
which identifies it as a "the model has learned the task" property that
ISLA reaches at 35 cases and the baselines at 210. At 1,260 cases it
collapses for both architectures — the remaining error is not
seed-dependent model variance — which is part of the evidence, taken up in
@sec-shared-floor, that both architectures approach a common floor at this
token count. Two-seed ensembles gain only 1–5% at any rung. Only the
ranking is tested here, not calibration.

## What carries it {#sec-mechanism}

ISLA differs from the Transolver family in several ways at once: exact
rotation and translation equivariance, an invariant seed parameterization,
measure-weighted routing, equivariant slice anchors with relational
invariants, and an optional similarity gauge. Removing one at a time at
35 cases (reference ISLA error 0.138) gives:

| single-factor change to ISLA at 35 cases | error (seed 42 / 43) | vs reference |
|---|---|---|
| add raw coordinates as inputs (breaks exact equivariance) | 0.143 / 0.143 | 1.04x |
| replace the invariant seeds by the raw vectors [r, n, d] | 0.138 / 0.137 | 0.99x |
| similarity gauge on | 0.151 / 0.147 | 1.08x |
| measure weights off | 0.121 / 0.123 | **0.88x** |
| relational routing off in the encoder | 0.158 / 0.163 | 1.16x |

: Single-factor ablations of ISLA at 35 training cases, two seeds, frozen protocol, shared validation set. Every variant retains an invariant path somewhere (the relational invariants in the encoder, or in the decoder read blocks), so these results speak to exactness and to individual ingredients, not to the presence of invariant information. Data: results/a35_v0_reduction_2026-09-05.json. {#tbl-hilift-ablations}

No single ingredient carries the advantage: nothing moves the error by
more than 16%, against a 190% gap to the baselines. Exactness of the
equivariance is not load-bearing (adding raw coordinates costs 4%); the
invariant seed set is not (raw vectors cost nothing); the gauge is neutral
to slightly harmful at this rung; and measure weights, which buy
sampling-density robustness (@sec-robustness-density), *cost* 12% at 35
cases, where uniform sampling makes area weights a source of gradient
variance rather than information. Relational routing is worth 16%.

The complementary test from the baseline side gives GeoTransolver and
Transolver ISLA's three drive-relative invariants (local incidence n·d,
radial cosine, radius) as per-cell input features at 35 cases, with bands
fixed in advance: the inputs carry the advantage if both baselines reach
0.235 or better (halfway to ISLA in log-error), and do not if both stay at
0.30 or worse. Transolver improves from 0.402 to 0.297 (a 1.35x gain, a
quarter of the log-gap, inside the inconclusive band); GeoTransolver does
not move (0.392 to 0.394, in the falsifier band). The invariant inputs are
therefore not the carrier for GeoTransolver and at most a partial
contributor for Transolver.^[`results/inv_transplant_2026-09-07.json`]
The single-angle split settles *where* the advantage lives. The dataset's
`single_aoa_12` split holds 126 geometries at one angle of attack (12°) and
validates on 18 geometries never seen at any angle. If ISLA's edge came from
representing the freestream-direction dependence, it should vanish here; the
preregistered bar was GeoTransolver/ISLA ≤ 1.25, with ≥ 1.67 as the
falsifier. Measured: ISLA 0.035 / 0.036 against GeoTransolver 0.175 / 0.183
— **5.0x**, on 18 of 18 held-out geometries (per-geometry ratios 4.0–6.4),
with lift to 0.6% and drag to 1.6% against 2.0% and 3.9%.^[`results/w2_reduction_2026-09-07.json`,
arm `D_single_aoa_12`.] Fixing the angle makes the gap *larger*, not
smaller: the matched-size mixed-angle control (126 cases at all angles, the
shared 180-case validation set) gives ISLA 0.077 and GeoTransolver 0.226
(3.0x), so fixing the angle halves ISLA's error at equal training-set size
and leaves GeoTransolver's nearly unchanged. What ISLA does with few samples is generalize across high-lift
*geometries* — flap and slat settings and the gaps between elements — and
GeoTransolver, from 126 distinct geometries at one operating point, has not
begun to (its error there, 0.18, is where it also sits at 35 mixed cases).
Plain Transolver on the same split scores 0.087 and 0.096 (mean 0.091): 1.96x
ahead of GeoTransolver and 2.55x behind ISLA, so of GeoTransolver's
fixed-angle deficit about two fifths (in log-error) is its geometry-encoder
path and the remaining 2.5x is the slice-attention backbone both baselines
share (results/w2_reduction_2026-09-08b.json, arm
`D_single_aoa_12_transolver`; preregistered bands at 2.0x and 3.5x, so the
split between the two is measured, not decided).
The DrivAerML contrast fits this reading: smooth single-body morphs of one
car, where GeoTransolver is 1.2–1.3x ahead, are not the kind of geometry
variation on which ISLA's routing has an advantage. Which ingredient of the
soft-slice design carries that geometry generalization is still not
isolated; the first rung of the unseen-geometry ladder is in
@sec-de-strata (1.8x on 18 never-seen geometries from four training
geometries); a GeoTransolver learning-rate steel-man at the single angle
made GeoTransolver worse (0.280 at 3e-3 against 0.179 at 1e-3, so the 5.0x
is stated at its better rate; results/w2_reduction_2026-09-08.json); the
ladder's 210-case rung is not yet measured (@sec-program-status).

## The same protocol on DrivAerML {#sec-de-drivaerml}

The advantage does not transfer to DrivAerML. Its data-efficiency ladder
(@sec-datasets) trains both architectures on nested subsets of the 435-car
training split — 14, 27, 54, 109 and 218 cars — under the frozen protocol
of that ladder, learning rate 3e-3 for both, 500 epochs, 10,000 tokens, two
seeds, scored on the 48-car validation split.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-drivaerml-dataeff-ladder
#| output: asis
#| code-fold: true
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
lad = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "ladder_reduction.json"))
print("| training cars | GeoTransolver | ISLA | GT / ISLA |")
print("|---|---|---|---|")
for n in (14, 27, 54, 109, 218):
    g = [lad[f"lad_gt_n{n}_seed{s}"]["infamily"] for s in (42, 43)]
    m = [lad[f"lad_mt2_n{n}_seed{s}"]["infamily"] for s in (42, 43)]
    gm, mm = statistics.mean(g), statistics.mean(m)
    print(f"| {n} | {gm:.3f} ({min(g):.3f}–{max(g):.3f}) | {mm:.3f} ({min(m):.3f}–{max(m):.3f}) | {gm/mm:.2f} |")
print()
print(": DrivAerML data-efficiency ladder: surface-pressure relative L2 on the 48 validation cars, seed mean (seed range), at learning rate 3e-3 for both architectures (the frozen protocol of that ladder; ISLA's preferred rate of 1e-3 is worth about 1.1x at full data and does not change the ordering). GT / ISLA below one means GeoTransolver is more accurate. Data: results/ladder_reduction.json. {#tbl-drivaerml-dataeff-ladder}")
```

At 14 cars the two architectures tie at 0.27; from 27 cars up GeoTransolver is 1.2–1.3x more accurate, a gap that
persists to the full split (1.085x at each architecture's best rate,
@sec-full-data). The HiLift advantage is therefore a property of that
dataset's variation — 180 geometries crossed with ten angles of attack —
and not of small training sets in general. The same 1.2x appears on the
interior: trained on 54 cars, GeoTransolver's volume configuration leads
ISLA's query-token configuration by 1.21x on interior pressure, and the two
reach parity only at 435 cars (@sec-interior). On DrivAerML the deficit is
uniform in every way measured: the same on every third of the car
(@sec-limits-mechanism), a near-constant factor per car on a difficulty
ordering both architectures share (@tbl-hilift-percase-rho), unchanged by a
wider ISLA, and the same for the surface and the volume. Why the two
datasets differ is not known; the one mechanism hypothesis tested
(@sec-mechanism) did not explain it.

## Limits of the claim {#sec-de-limits}

**It is a data-efficiency claim, not a scaling law.** The measured
log-log slopes of error against training cases are 0.50 then 0.74 for
GeoTransolver and 0.43 then 0.25 for ISLA over the 35→210 and 210→1,260
segments: GeoTransolver's curve steepens where ISLA's flattens, and a naive
power-law extrapolation of the two curves puts GeoTransolver at 0.015 and
ISLA at 0.029 at 5,000 cases, a factor of two in GeoTransolver's favour.
The book makes no claim beyond 1,260 cases. Three pieces of evidence
suggest the flattening is a shared floor of the protocol rather than a
property of ISLA — 70% of the residual at full data is shared between the
two architectures on identical points, the seed-disagreement correlation
collapses for both at 1,260 cases, and accuracy still rises with tokens
per case — but that reading is a hypothesis under test (both architectures
at 1,260 cases with 20,000 tokens), not a result (@sec-shared-floor).

**It is one dataset.** On DrivAerML the ordering reverses
(@sec-de-drivaerml): GeoTransolver is 1.2–1.3x more accurate from 27
training cases up and the two tie at 14. The contrast with HiLiftAeroML,
where the angle of attack varies, is real and unexplained: the obvious
hypothesis (that ISLA wins by representing the freestream-direction
dependence exactly) predicts that giving the baselines those features would
close the gap, and it does not.

**It is in-distribution, and it is a validation-set figure.** The
validation cases are random draws from the same 180-geometry, ten-angle
design as the training cases; the checkpoints are final-epoch, with no
selection on validation error, but the sealed test split has been spent
only on regime extrapolation and one mechanism test, so no held-out
evaluation of the 35-case models exists yet. What happens
across a regime boundary is the subject of @sec-regime-extrapolation, and
the answer there is that no architecture generalizes.

**The mechanism is located but not isolated.** The advantage is geometry
generalization on multi-element high-lift configurations, largest when the
angle of attack is fixed; which ingredient of ISLA's design carries it is
not identified, as @sec-mechanism states.
